title: Health and safety legislation
summary: Explains the difference between statutory and non-statutory health and safety rules, the main regulations affecting electricians, and the consequences of breaking them.

sections.heading: Statutory and non-statutory rules
paragraphs: Employers and employees both need to understand health and safety regulations, and that includes you. Acts of Parliament are statutory, which means they are legally binding and enforceable by law. Certain Regulations are made under Acts and so are also statutory.

Other Regulations are advisory or guidance only. These are non-statutory and cannot be enforced by law, but they are generally seen as good practice and may be cited in a court of law. Many are based on statutory rules, so breaking them could mean a law has been broken somewhere.
bullets: Statutory: binding in law, and it is a criminal act to contravene it.
Non-statutory: not legally binding, but reflects good practice and may be cited in court.

sections.heading: Key definitions
paragraphs: Knowing who is who on site helps you understand who owes duties to whom.
bullets: Employer: a person or body that employs one or more persons under a contract of employment.
Employee: a person employed by an employer under a contract of employment.
Self-employed: anyone who works for gain or reward other than under a contract of employment.
Visitors to site: any person who comes on to site who is not usually there, so is unlikely to know its health and safety requirements.
Client: the person or organisation that instigated the work; may be the direct customer or the company a subcontractor works for.
Organisation: businesses, companies and corporate entities.
Individuals: employers, employees, contractors and visitors to site.
Health and safety materials: Acts of Parliament, Regulations and Approved Codes of Practice.

sections.heading: Main statutory regulations (part 1)
paragraphs: Many statutory regulations apply to the building services industry. The list is not exhaustive, and others can apply to specific types of work or working environments.
bullets: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974: covers all places where work is carried out. The 'etc.' was added to cover voluntary work. All persons are responsible for their own and others' safety.
Electricity at Work Regulations 1989: 33 regulations, of which 1-16 and 29 are the most relevant to most electricians. A statutory document.
COSHH: covers anything used at work that could be hazardous to health, such as chemicals, cements, oils and sprays.
Work at Height Regulations 2005: more people are killed and injured by falls than any other cause.
PPE at Work Regulations: an assessment of PPE requirements must be carried out, the employer must supply PPE and the employee must wear it.
Lifting and Manual Handling Operations Regulations: aim to reduce injury and ill health caused by manual handling of loads.
Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations: equipment must be safe to use and used safely.
Control of Asbestos at Work Regulations: asbestos is extremely dangerous when disturbed, and any possible exposure or presence should be reported immediately.

sections.heading: Main statutory regulations (part 2)
paragraphs: Employers have a general duty under section 2 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 to ensure, as far as is reasonably practicable, the health, safety and welfare of their employees. The Workplace (Health, Safety and Welfare) Regulations expand on this and aim to meet the needs of all the workforce, including people with disabilities.
bullets: Workplace regulations: protect everyone in the workplace and make sure adequate welfare facilities are provided; workstations should be accessible for disabled people.
First Aid Regulations: employers must make adequate first aid provision in case employees become ill or injured at work.
Control of Noise at Work Regulations: employers must reduce the risk to employees' health by controlling the noise they are exposed to.
Environmental Protection Act: defines the structure and authority for waste management and control of emissions into the environment.

Confined Spaces Regulations: a confined space is any enclosed place (such as a vessel, tank, pit, chamber or cellar) where conditions give a likelihood of an accident needing emergency action, for example flammable or explosive atmospheres, harmful gas, fume or vapour, free-flowing solids, rising liquid, too much or too little oxygen, or excessively high temperature.
CDM Regulations: place duties on clients, designers and contractors so health and safety is considered throughout a construction project, from inception to final demolition and removal.
Hazardous Waste Regulations: ensure waste is recovered or disposed of without endangering human health or harming the environment.

sections.heading: Waste and pollution regulations
paragraphs: WEEE covers waste electrical and electronic equipment such as computers, TVs, fridges and phones, one of the fastest growing waste streams in the EU. The first WEEE Directive came into force in February 2003 and set up schemes where consumers return spent appliances free of charge, to increase recycling and re-use. The revised directive came into effect on 14th February 2014.

The Pollution Prevention Control (PPC) Act improves energy efficiency and prevents pollution in energy-intensive industry through a single permitting process. A company carrying out any activity covered by PPC must hold a PPC permit issued by an environmental regulator or local council.
bullets: PPC requirements apply to industrial sites accounting for about 60% of the energy use of the manufacturing industry, plus energy supply industries such as power plants and refineries.

sections.heading: Non-statutory guidance
paragraphs: BS 7671 is published by the IET and is the national standard for low voltage electrical installations in the UK. In 1992 the IEE Wiring Regulations became British Standard BS 7671. They are non-statutory, but are referenced in several UK statutory instruments.

Approved Codes of Practice give practical guidance on compliance. Failing to follow one is not an offence in itself, but if someone is prosecuted and it is proved the Code was not followed, a court can regard that as evidence of guilt unless they complied with the law in some other way. Following them is best practice.
bullets: HSE guidance publications explain how to interpret and implement Regulations; they are not the Regulations themselves.
IET On-Site Guide: a handy handbook for electricians on building sites, containing some information not found in BS 7671.

sections.heading: Consequences of non-compliance
paragraphs: Breaking statutory regulations has direct legal consequences and wider knock-on effects.
bullets: Direct: prosecution, fine, imprisonment.
Prohibition notice: the work activity or premises must not be used until the non-compliance is rectified.
Improvement notice: the activity or premises can carry on being used, but shortcomings must be rectified within a specified time.
Non-direct: dismissal, injury, death, loss of earnings, lost clients and loss of reputation.

flashcards.back: Binding in law; it is a criminal act to contravene it. Acts of Parliament and Regulations made under them are statutory.
Not legally binding, but generally good practice and may be cited in court. Many are based on statutory rules.
Anyone who works for gain or reward other than under a contract of employment.

flashcards.front: Why was 'etc.' added to the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act?
flashcards.back: To cover voluntary work, as well as all other places where work is carried out.

flashcards.front: Which regulations of the Electricity at Work Regulations matter most to electricians?
flashcards.back: There are 33 regulations in total; numbers 1-16 and 29 are the most relevant to most electricians.
Anything used in the workplace that could be hazardous to health, such as chemicals, cements, oils and sprays.

flashcards.front: What are the three PPE duties under the PPE at Work Regulations?
flashcards.back: An assessment of PPE requirements must be carried out, the employer must supply the PPE, and the employee must wear it.

flashcards.front: What should you do about possible asbestos?
flashcards.back: Report any possible exposure to, or presence of, asbestos immediately, because it is extremely dangerous when disturbed.

flashcards.front: What do the CDM Regulations aim to achieve?
flashcards.back: They place duties on clients, designers and contractors so health and safety is considered throughout a construction project, from inception to final demolition.
The national standard for low voltage electrical installations in the UK, published by the IET. It is non-statutory but referenced in several statutory instruments.

flashcards.front: What is the legal status of an Approved Code of Practice?
flashcards.back: Not following it is not an offence itself, but in a prosecution a court can treat it as evidence of guilt unless you complied with the law another way.
Prohibition: the activity or premises must not be used until rectified. Improvement: use may continue but shortcomings must be fixed within a specified time.

quiz.q: What does it mean if a regulation is described as statutory?
options: It is binding in law and breaking it is a criminal act
It is published by the IET
quiz.why: Statutory means binding in law, and it is a criminal act to contravene it.

quiz.q: Which of these is a non-statutory document?
options: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974
Control of Asbestos at Work Regulations
quiz.why: The Wiring Regulations (BS 7671) are non-statutory, although they are referenced in several statutory instruments.

quiz.q: Which Electricity at Work Regulations are most relevant to most electricians?
quiz.why: Of the 33 regulations, 1-16 and 29 are the most relevant to most electricians.

quiz.q: Under the PPE at Work Regulations, who must supply the PPE?
quiz.why: The employer must supply PPE, and the employee must wear it.

quiz.q: You suspect a ceiling void contains asbestos. What should you do?
options: Carry on carefully so you do not disturb it
Wait until the end of the job
Remove it yourself using a dust mask
quiz.why: Asbestos is extremely dangerous when disturbed, and any possible exposure or presence should be reported immediately.

quiz.q: Which regulations place duties on clients, designers and contractors across the whole life of a construction project?
quiz.why: CDM Regulations make health and safety a consideration from the start of a project to final demolition and removal.

quiz.q: Which regulations aim to increase recycling of spent appliances such as fridges and computers by schemes that let consumers return them free of charge?
options: Control of Noise at Work Regulations
Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Regulations
quiz.why: WEEE schemes allow consumers to return spent electrical equipment free of charge to increase recycling and re-use.

quiz.q: A company has failed to follow an Approved Code of Practice and faces prosecution. What is the effect in court?
options: It can be regarded as evidence of guilt unless the law was complied with in some other way
Nothing, because it is not a law
quiz.why: Approved Codes of Practice have special legal status, and failure to follow one can be seen as evidence of guilt.

quiz.q: An inspector issues a notice that lets work carry on but requires shortcomings to be fixed within a set time. What is it?
quiz.why: An improvement notice allows the activity to continue while shortcomings are rectified in a specified time period.

quiz.q: Which of these is a non-direct implication of breaking statutory regulations?
quiz.why: Loss of reputation is listed as a non-direct implication, along with dismissal, injury, death, loss of earnings and lost clients.

quiz.q: Which regulations ensure waste is recovered or disposed of without endangering human health or harming the environment?
options: Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations
quiz.why: The Hazardous Waste Regulations exist to ensure waste is disposed of without harming people or the environment.

quiz.q: Which cause does the deck say kills and injures more people than any other?
quiz.why: The Work at Height Regulations note that more people are killed and injured by falls than any other cause.
